Zeno of Elea. Around four hundred and ninety to four hundred and thirty BCE. He was a Greek philosopher and student of Parmenides who invented a battery of paradoxes to defend his teacher's claim that motion and plurality are illusory. His paradoxes—the Dichotomy, Achilles and the Tortoise, the Arrow, and others—have fascinated mathematicians and philosophers for twenty-five centuries.

Zeno lived in Elea, southern Italy, and devoted his career to defending Parmenides against critics. We know him entirely through reports by later philosophers, chiefly Aristotle. He invented no positive doctrine of his own. His method was reductio ad absurdum. He would assume that motion exists, then derive a contradiction. Socrates praised his ingenuity in Plato's Parmenides dialogue.

His first paradox is the Dichotomy. To move from A to B, one must first reach the midpoint. But to reach the midpoint, one must reach its midpoint, and so on infinitely. So motion can never begin. Next is Achilles and the Tortoise. The swift Achilles chases a slow tortoise. Before Achilles catches it, he must first reach where it was. But by then it has moved forward. Achilles repeats this process infinitely, never catching up. Then the Arrow. An arrow in flight must occupy space equal to itself. Only what occupies space equal to itself is at rest. Therefore, the arrow is at rest. Motion is an illusion. Finally, the Stadium, also called the Dichotomy of Space. Parallel reasoning about space itself. Similar infinite regress.

Aristotle critiqued Zeno, arguing that infinite series can have finite sums. The dichotomy sums to a finite distance. Modern calculus and the concept of limits vindicate Aristotle's intuition. Infinite series converge. Yet Zeno's paradoxes remain profound. They expose conceptual tensions between the discrete and continuous, between the infinite and the finite.

Zeno's paradoxes exemplify philosophy's power to reveal hidden contradictions in apparent truisms. Common sense says motion is real, objects are plural. But these lead to logical contradiction. They defend Parmenides' monism. If plurality and motion generate paradoxes, perhaps his one unchanging Being is correct. Though Parmenidean monism is now rejected, Zeno's arguments remain brilliant exemplars of the reductio ad absurdum method. His paradoxes recur in quantum mechanics, in the measurement problem, in relativity, in computational theory. They show that the infinite is not marginal but central to understanding motion, time, and space.
